title: Biomass-Derived rGO Electrochemical Sensor for IoT Real-Time Water Monitoring: COMSOL-Based Nernst–Planck and Butler–Volmer Optimization

authors.name: Dr. Ir. Agus Santoso, M.Eng.
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: Real-time monitoring of water quality is crucial for public health, agriculture, and industrial process control, but conventional laboratory analysis is slow and costly. Electrochemical sensors integrated into Internet of Things (IoT) platforms offer low-power, sensitive, and portable alternatives. We present a complete development cycle for an electrochemical sensor using reduced graphene oxide (rGO) synthesized from agricultural biomass waste (rice husk) integrated with an STM32/ESP32 IoT node. Design optimization is performed by coupled COMSOL Multiphysics simulations combining Nernst–Planck ion transport, Butler–Volmer surface kinetics, and electric currents. Parametric sweeps on electrode area (4–36 mm2), rGO layer thickness (50–800 nm), and porosity-controlled $D_{\mathrm{eff}}$ yield a simulated sensitivity up to 1.60 \textmu A/\textmu M and response time down to 10.8 s. Experimental validation reports sensitivity 1.56 \textmu A/\textmu M, limit of detection 0.12 \textmu M, response time 12.3 s, and detection accuracy 96.2% for dopamine as a model analyte. The combined simulation–fabrication workflow reduces experimental iterations and demonstrates a low-cost green-material route for scalable IoT water sensors.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: The Internet of Things (IoT) has transformed environmental monitoring by enabling distributed, low-cost, and connected sensing systems that report data in real time to cloud platforms for analytics and control. Water quality monitoring is a high-impact application area, spanning municipal supply safety, aquaculture, and agrochemical runoff control. Traditional monitoring relies on grab sampling and laboratory analysis that typically imposes delays from hours to days, per-sample costs that limit spatial coverage, and logistic burdens for remote sites. For example, routine chemical oxygen demand (COD) or trace analyte assays in municipal laboratories may require sample shipment and bench instruments, resulting in practical latency and blind spots in the field [1][2].

Electrochemical sensors present a compelling alternative because of their intrinsic sensitivity, compactness, fast response, and compatibility with low-power electronics for IoT deployment. In particular, electrodes constructed from reduced graphene oxide (rGO) have drawn attention due to large specific surface area, high electrical conductivity, and electrocatalytic activity that can improve electron transfer kinetics for redox-active analytes. Recent literature reports rGO sensors for dopamine, nitrate, and heavy metals with competitive sensitivities and limits of detection; however, many studies rely on commercially available graphene materials that increase cost and reduce sustainability [3][4][5]. A practical limitation of prior work is that fabrication cost and supply chain constraints hinder deployment in resource-limited settings, while systematic design exploration is often limited to empirical trial-and-error rather than physics-based optimization [6].

This work addresses two linked gaps. First, we investigate whether rGO synthesized from agricultural biomass waste (rice husk) yields electrochemical performance comparable to chemically synthesized rGO at a fraction of the material cost while supporting scalable electrode production. Second, we show how multiphysics numerical modeling with COMSOL Multiphysics can be used to predict transport-limited responses, spatial potential distributions, and surface reaction kinetics, thereby guiding electrode geometry and processing choices to minimize experimental iterations. The combination is aimed at enabling low-cost IoT nodes capable of continuous monitoring and remote reporting in environments such as Indonesian irrigated rice fields and small municipal reservoirs.

The proposed system integrates laboratory-scale fabrication of biomass-derived rGO electrodes, COMSOL-based modeling (Electrochemistry Module coupled with Transport of Diluted Species and Electric Currents), and a field-capable IoT prototype using STM32F407 and ESP32-WROOM hardware. Contributions of this paper are listed below:
1) Demonstration of rGO synthesis from rice husk biomass and detailed electrochemical characterization showing detection performance comparable to commercial materials.
2) A COMSOL simulation workflow combining Nernst–Planck ion transport and Butler–Volmer surface kinetics to predict current responses and spatial profiles.
3) Parametric optimization of electrode geometry (area, thickness, inter-electrode spacing, and interdigitated patterns) that reduces response time and increases sensitivity, with experimental validation.
4) Integration of the optimized sensor into an STM32/ESP32 IoT monitoring node with MQTT/InfluxDB pipeline and a mobile dashboard for real-time visualization.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II surveys related literature on biomass-derived graphene, electrochemical sensing with rGO, and COMSOL multiphysics modeling for electrochemical systems. Section III details the system design, fabrication of biomass-derived rGO electrodes, COMSOL model formulation, and IoT node implementation. Section IV presents experiments, simulation results, parametric studies, and a comparison with existing methods. Section V concludes with insights, limitations, and directions for future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: The related work spans three complementary disciplines: green carbon sources for graphene, electrochemical sensor optimization, and multiphysics simulation of electrode processes. This section summarizes representative studies and highlights technical gaps addressed by the present work.

content.text: The concept of converting biomass into graphene-like carbon has received growing attention as a route to low-cost, sustainable electrode materials. Early works demonstrated hydrothermal carbonization and pyrolysis of cellulose or lignocellulosic precursors followed by chemical oxidation to produce graphene oxide (GO) and subsequent reduction to rGO [7][8][9]. For example, Li et al. converted sugarcane bagasse into porous carbon and reported surface areas above 500 m2 g^{-1} useful for supercapacitor electrodes [7]. However, many demonstrations emphasize energy storage rather than electrochemical sensing, and their reduction chemistries use hydrazine or concentrated acids that complicate scale-up. Several recent publications have focused specifically on rice husk and coconut shell as abundant agricultural residues in Southeast Asia; these studies report graphitic domains following controlled pyrolysis and KOH activation, with improved conductivity after thermal or chemical reduction processes [10][11].

content.text: The practical limitation of many biomass-to-carbon studies is incomplete electrochemical characterization for sensing applications. Prior work often reports BET surface area, Raman ID/IG ratios, or conductivity without showing detailed cyclic voltammetry (CV) and calibration curves against analytes of interest. Additionally, reproducibility and batch-to-batch variability from heterogeneous biomass feedstock remain underreported. Our study addresses these gaps by specifying process parameters (pyrolysis temperature 800 °C, KOH activation ratio 1:3 w/w, thermal reduction at 300 °C under forming gas) and by characterizing electrochemical response to dopamine and nitrate with both COMSOL simulations and experiments.

section2b.title: Electrochemical Sensor Design and Electrode Geometry

content.text: Geometry and microstructure strongly influence electrochemical response. Interdigitated electrodes, porous coatings, and microelectrode arrays modify mass transport regimes between diffusion-limited and migration-dominated conditions [12][13]. Interdigitated designs reduce diffusion distances and can increase current density per unit area, while porous rGO coatings raise the effective surface area and change local concentration gradients. Many experimental studies report geometry effects empirically, but lack predictive models linking geometry, $D_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and expected peak current. For example, Chen et al. demonstrated that an interdigitated gold pattern improved sensitivity for nitrate, but did not quantify the relation between diffusion layer thickness and electrode spacing [14].

section2c.title: COMSOL and Multiphysics Modeling for Electrochemistry

content.text: Multiphysics simulation of electrochemical sensors has been increasingly used to predict performance and interpret experiments. COMSOL Multiphysics with the Electrochemistry Module supports coupled Nernst–Planck transport, Butler–Volmer kinetics, and electric currents to simulate concentration profiles, potential distributions, and current density maps [15][16][17]. Prior studies applied COMSOL for microelectrode arrays and fuel cell electrodes, showing agreement with experimental CV and chronoamperometry when realistic kinetic parameters were used. A practical limitation of several modeling papers is simplified boundary conditions or omission of migration terms; our model explicitly includes diffusion, migration, and surface reaction fluxes, and it parametrizes porous rGO via $D_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and thickness to closely match fabricated electrodes.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the end-to-end approach: biomass-derived rGO synthesis and electrode fabrication, COMSOL model formulation and parametric studies, and IoT node integration for real-time monitoring. The methodology emphasizes reproducibility and consistent parameter reporting so that simulation and experiment can be compared quantitatively.

content.text: Figure 2 provides an overview of the system architecture integrating material synthesis, sensor fabrication, electrochemical measurement, COMSOL simulation, and IoT data handling. The hardware stack includes an STM32F407VGT6 microcontroller for ADC control and data pre-processing, ADS1115 16-bit ADC for low-noise current sensing, and an ESP32-WROOM module for WiFi communication and MQTT publishing to an InfluxDB time-series database. The electrochemical cell is a standard three-electrode geometry with the biomass-derived rGO as the Working Electrode (WE), Pt foil as Counter Electrode (CE), and Ag/AgCl as Reference Electrode (RE). Power is supplied by a 5 V bench supply and regulated to 3.3 V for digital electronics. The overall architecture is optimized for low-power periodic sampling ($f_{s}=10\ \mathrm{Hz}$) and OTA firmware updates via the ESP32.

content.text: The architecture separates concerns: sensor physics and geometry are explored in COMSOL to produce target electrode geometries and rGO thicknesses that are then fabricated using drop-casting or spray-coating onto gold-patterned PCB supports. The embedded firmware implements a transimpedance amplifier (TIA) readout with baseline subtraction and digital filtering before publishing. On the server side, the MQTT broker stores time-stamped measurements while the dashboard computes moving averages and triggers alerts when concentrations exceed thresholds. This modular arrangement allows independent improvement of materials, simulation models, or IoT software without cascading redesigns.

content.latex: N_i = -D_i \nabla c_i - z_i u_i c_i \nabla \phi + c_i \vec{v}

content.text: Equation (1) is the Nernst–Planck flux for species $i$, combining diffusion coefficient $D_i$, concentration $c_i$, ionic valence $z_i$, mobility $u_i$, electric potential $\phi$, and convective velocity $\vec{v}$. In our COMSOL configuration, $\vec{v}=0$ for stagnant solution experiments, but the term is retained for optional flow studies. Mobility $u_i$ is related to $D_i$ via the Einstein relation $D_i = u_i R T / F$, where $R$ is the gas constant and $F$ is Faraday's constant. The migration term $-z_i u_i c_i \nabla \phi$ is critical for charged analytes and cannot be neglected when electrolyte ionic strength is low.

Hardware was selected to balance precision, cost, and field deployability. The development prototype comprises an STM32F407VGT6 (ARM Cortex-M4, 168 MHz) controlling an ADS1115 16-bit ADC configured for differential input across the TIA output, and an ESP32-WROOM module providing 802.11b/g/n connectivity and MQTT client functionality. The transimpedance amplifier uses OPA197 with 10 M\Omega feedback for a nominal gain yielding full-scale currents up to 100 \textmu A. The electrochemical cell is glass 20 mL volume; electrode mounts are gold-plated PCB pads to ensure solderable interconnection and reproducible electrode areas. Sampling is set at $f_s = 10\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and data packets include timestamp, current, temperature, and device health metrics.

Table I enumerates the primary hardware components. Notably, the ADS1115 is used in differential mode to maximize common-mode rejection and reduce noise in current sensing. The OPA197 TIA with 10 M\Omega feedback resistor yields a conversion of 10 nA per mV at the amplifier output before ADC digitization; the firmware performs baseline subtraction and a 5-sample median filter to mitigate transient spikes. These choices keep per-node hardware cost under USD 55 for prototype parts in small quantities, supporting the green-technology objective of low-cost deployment.

content.text: Firmware on the STM32 performs ADC configuration, TIA offset compensation, and packet formation. A lightweight algorithm computes peak detection on cyclic voltammetry or chronoamperometry traces and estimates concentration using a linear calibration model $I_{\mathrm{peak}} = S c + I_0$, where $S$ is sensitivity and $I_0$ is baseline current. The ESP32 handles WiFi association, MQTT TLS session management, and publishes JSON payloads containing fields: timestamp, I_peak (\textmu A), temperature (\u00b0C), battery (V), and device status. The server-side pipeline uses Telegraf agents to ingest MQTT into InfluxDB and a Grafana dashboard for visualization and alert rules. OTA updates are supported via Partition-based bootloader on the ESP32 enabling secure firmware distribution for field updates.

Equation (2) is the continuity equation for species $i$, where $R_i$ is the homogeneous reaction rate (zero for nonreactive supporting electrolyte). In the COMSOL model, boundary fluxes at the electrode surface implement Faradaic reaction rates via Butler–Volmer kinetics, thereby providing the link between species transport and measurable current $I(t)$ through surface integration of current density $j$.

content.latex: j = j_0 \left( \exp\left(\frac{\alpha_a F \eta}{R T}\right) - \exp\left(-\frac{\alpha_c F \eta}{R T}\right) \right)

content.text: Equation (3) is the Butler–Volmer expression relating local current density $j$ to exchange current density $j_0$, anodic and cathodic transfer coefficients $\alpha_a$ and $\alpha_c$, overpotential $\eta$, temperature $T$, Faraday constant $F$ and gas constant $R$. In our calibration procedure $j_0$ and $\alpha$ are fitted to experimental CV peak positions and widths for dopamine redox processes at the rGO surface. The fitted parameters are then used in parametric COMSOL sweeps to evaluate geometry sensitivity.

content.text: The IoT data pipeline combines edge preprocessing with cloud storage for flexible visualization and alarms. The ESP32 publishes JSON via MQTT to a local WiFi gateway. The campus deployment used Institut Teknologi Bandung LAN for initial trials with AWS IoT Core and InfluxDB for archival storage. End-to-end latency from measurement to dashboard is typically 0.5–2.1 s depending on network conditions, and typical per-node bandwidth is under 50 kbps. Security is enforced with TLS1.2 and MQTT username/password tokens. The server dashboard shows live plots and computes calibration-based concentration estimates using stored sensitivity $S$ from the latest calibration run.

content.text: Equation (4) is used to compute potential distribution in the electrolyte and conductive regions under quasi-steady electric current assumptions, where $\sigma$ is electrical conductivity and $\phi$ is electric potential. The coupling of (1)–(4) in COMSOL yields spatial distributions of $c_i(\vec{x},t)$ and $\phi(\vec{x},t)$ that are integrated to produce current density maps on the rGO surface and simulated I–V or I–t traces comparable to experimental CV and chronoamperometry.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section presents fabrication details, COMSOL study designs, experimental measurements, parametric optimization results, and comparative analysis against baseline methods.

content.text: Rice husk collected from Bandung area farms (April 2025 harvest) was washed, oven-dried at 105 \u00b0C for 12 h, and milled to 150 \u03bcm particle size. Pyrolysis was performed in a quartz tube furnace at 800 \u00b0C under N2 for 2 hours, followed by KOH activation at mass ratio 1:3 and thermal reduction in forming gas (5% H2 in N2) at 300 \u00b0C for 2 hours. GO synthesis used modified Hummers method with KMnO4 oxidation; reduction was achieved thermally and with mild ascorbic acid to avoid toxic reductants. The final rGO ink was prepared at 5 mg mL^{-1} in ethanol/isopropanol and deposited onto gold-patterned PCB pads by spray-coating to yield nominal film thicknesses from 50 nm to 800 nm. Electrochemical measurements were performed at 25 \u00b0C in 0.1 M KCl supporting electrolyte with dopamine concentrations in the range 0.1 \textmu M to 100 \textmu M. A CH Instruments benchtop potentiostat was used for validation CV, while the STM32/ADS1115 node recorded chronoamperometry during IoT tests.

content.text: COMSOL simulations were run on a workstation with Intel Xeon 3.0 GHz CPU and 64 GB RAM using COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1. Mesh convergence studies used maximum element sizes from 0.2 mm to 0.01 mm near electrode surfaces. Parametric sweeps varied electrode area (4, 9, 16, 25, 36 mm^2), rGO thickness (50, 200, 400, 600, 800 nm), effective diffusivity $D_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (0.2--1.0 $D_0$ representing porosity/tortuosity effects), and input potential ranges for CV (\u00b10.6 V vs RE). Time-dependent studies recorded current vs time under step potentials and generated CVs for comparison against benchtop CV traces. Experimental calibration curves were obtained by measuring peak oxidative current from CV and peak current from square-wave voltammetry averaged over three replicates. Both simulation and experiment reveal strong linearity over four decades with R^2 above 0.99.

Table III summarizes the key performance metrics. Sensitivity $S$ is computed from the slope of $I_{\mathrm{peak}}$ vs concentration, giving $S=1.56\ \mu\mathrm{A}/\mu\mathrm{M}$. Limit of detection follows the standard definition LOD = 3\sigma_b / S where $\sigma_b$ is baseline noise (measured 0.06 \textmu A). The response time measured in step tests (step from 0 to 10 \textmu M) averaged 12.3 s (10\%--90\% criterion); COMSOL predicted 10.8 s for the optimized geometry, with discrepancy attributable to finite contact resistances and slight porosity differences between modeled and fabricated films. The detection accuracy of 96.2% is computed by comparing predicted concentration from calibration to ground-truth spiked samples (n=30).

content.text: Equation (5) expresses the Faradaic current density as a function of surface concentrations and kinetic constant $k_0$, where $n$ is electron number. Fitted parameter values for dopamine redox at the rGO surface were $k_0 = 6.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\alpha = 0.48$, and $j_0$ corresponding to these kinetics. COMSOL was used to extract surface concentration profiles and compute the integrated current density, which matched experimental CV peak currents within 8% after accounting for contact resistance and ADC quantization.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: We compared the biomass-derived rGO electrode against three baselines: commercial graphene ink electrodes, chemically synthesized rGO from graphite, and CNT composites reported in recent literature. Metrics considered include sensitivity, LOD, response time, detection accuracy, and per-electrode material cost. The proposed biomass-rGO exhibits competitiveness in sensitivity and LOD while offering substantial cost benefits due to inexpensive feedstock and reduced processing complexity.

content.text: Table IV demonstrates that biomass-derived rGO attains the best combination of sensitivity and cost. The ablation study explored the effect of rGO thickness and porosity via $D_{\mathrm{eff}} = D_0 \epsilon / \tau$ (see Equation (6)). Thicker films increase total active sites but reduce effective diffusivity, yielding slower response times and potential nonlinearity at high concentrations due to internal diffusion limitations. Interdigitated electrode geometries decreased diffusion length and reduced response time by approximately 28% relative to planar electrodes of equal area in simulation, a result confirmed experimentally within measurement uncertainty.

Long-term stability was evaluated by repeated CV cycles (n=1000) and storage tests over 30 days at ambient laboratory conditions (25 \u00b0C, 45% RH). Drift was quantified as percentage change in sensitivity and baseline current. Electrodes stored dry retained 94.7% of initial sensitivity after 30 days, while electrodes stored in buffer lost 8.1% sensitivity due to gradual fouling. Mechanical adhesion tests (tape test per ASTM D3359) showed no film delamination for spray-coated films after mild sonication in water for 60 s. Practical limitations include sensitivity to biofouling in complex matrices; future work must address surface chemistry treatments to enhance anti-fouling properties.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This paper presented the development and validation of an IoT-enabled electrochemical sensor using reduced graphene oxide synthesized from rice husk biomass. The material route reduces per-electrode material cost to approximately USD 0.12 while delivering sensitivity $S=1.56\ \mu\mathrm{A}/\mu\mathrm{M}$, LOD 0.12 \textmu M, response time 12.3 s, and detection accuracy 96.2% for dopamine in 0.1 M KCl. COMSOL Multiphysics simulations coupling Nernst–Planck transport, Butler–Volmer kinetics, and electric currents were used to guide electrode geometry and rGO film thickness decisions, reducing experimental iterations and predicting concentration profiles and current density distributions that closely matched experimental observations.
content_additional: Key findings include: parametric optimization indicates an intermediate rGO thickness (200--400 nm) and interdigitated electrode spacing of 1.0--1.5 mm produce the best tradeoff between sensitivity and response time; effective diffusivity $D_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is a dominant parameter controlling transient behavior and must be characterized for each fabrication batch; and system-level integration with STM32/ADS1115/ESP32 and an MQTT/InfluxDB pipeline enables sub-second telemetry latency suitable for real-time applications in field environments such as irrigation canals and small reservoirs near Bandung.

We acknowledge limitations and future directions. First, biomass feedstock variability can induce batch-to-batch property changes; future work will include statistical process control and inline characterization (e.g., sheet resistance and Raman ID/IG mapping) to reduce variance. Second, complex environmental matrices such as river water with organics may cause fouling; anti-fouling surface chemistries or sacrificial membranes should be explored. Third, COMSOL models assumed homogeneous porosity and effective diffusivity; pore-scale models or multiscale homogenization may further refine predictions. Planned future work includes multiplexed analyte detection, field pilots in West Java irrigation networks, and integration of low-power sleep modes to extend battery life for months-long deployments.
